articles.title: Influence of COVID-19 and COVID-19 rumours on trust and uptake of single-dose male HPV vaccination in the Add-Vacc cluster-randomised trial, northwest Tanzania.
articles.summary: PMID: 42854550. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129231. BackgroundThe COVID-19 pandemic impacted public health services and vaccination uptake globally. Trust in health services and vaccination programmes is critical for vaccine acceptance. Between 2020 and 2022, Tanzania shifted its acknowledgement of COVID-19 and its prevention strategies. National COVID-19 vaccination coverage reached 51% by April 2023. The Add-Vacc cluster-randomised trial (CRT) provided single-dose, human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination to 14-18-year-old males in 2023-2024, the first time HPV vaccination was offered to young men in Tanzania. The Tanzania national vaccination programme promotes HPV vaccination for girls as the vaccine to prevent cervical cancer.ObjectiveThis qualitative study investigated the influence of vaccine and COVID-19 rumours on uptake of male HPV vaccination offered through the trial.MethodsBetween May 2023 to May 2024, field teams collected rumours data using an electronic-rumours tracking tool, key informant interviews, in-depth interviews, focus group discussions and rapid ethnography with stakeholders including adolescents, parents, teachers, health workers and community leaders.ResultsData from community members, including youth, indicated that changes in Tanzania's COVID-19 policies between 2020 and 2022 prompted mistrust and concerns about the trial vaccine. Documented concerns included questions regarding the motives of national leadership and vaccination programmes, rumours that the vaccine offered through the trial was a concealed COVID-19 vaccine or was for- depopulation or led to changes in fertility and/or male virility. Rapid assessment of trial-related rumours and responsive, ongoing community engagement activities to address rumours supported efforts to enhance vaccination uptake and acceptance.ConclusionShifting COVID-19 policies during the height of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic subsequently influenced trust and HPV vaccine acceptance during the vaccination phase of the Add-Vacc CRT. Documenting and monitoring community concerns early in a project delivering a vaccine to a new population group can inform ongoing, dynamic community engagement aimed towards promoting dialogue and building trust across stakeholder groups and implementation teams.

articles.title: Ethnic disparities in COVID-19 vaccine uptake among among 55+ year-old Canadians: Exploring the role of racial discrimination, chronic disease comorbidities, and conspiracy beliefs.
articles.summary: PMID: 42837895. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129213. BackgroundCanada's COVID-19 vaccination program achieved high overall coverage, yet older racialized and Indigenous people experienced lower uptake and far higher infection and mortality rates. Structural inequities, low health literacy, mistrust, and misinformation contributed to these gaps. Despite early vaccine prioritization, little disaggregated data exist for racialized and Indigenous older adults. This study examines vaccine uptake in these underserved groups to inform more equitable public health strategies and strengthen future pandemic responses.MethodsWe conducted a Canada-wide cross-sectional online survey of adults aged ≥55 years in March 2025 using Computer-Assisted Web Interviewing. Participants completed measures assessing COVID-19 vaccination doses, experiences of major racial discrimination, conspiracy beliefs, health literacy, chronic conditions, and sociodemographic characteristics.ResultsOf the 581participants, 90,3% received at least one dose. Black and Indigenous people were more often unvaccinated (17%), compared to 5.5-6% for Asians and Arabs. Receipt of ≥5 doses was observed in 50% of White, 41.8% of Asian and 13.8% of Black individuals. Older adults (≥65 years) had greater uptake (OR=1.58, 95%CI: 1.07-2.32), as did retirees (OR=2.47) and more highly educated participants (college OR=2.29; Bachelor OR=2.77). Higher conspiracy belief scores were significantly associated with lower odds of receiving higher doses (OR=0.91, 95%CI: 0.89-0.93; p<0.001). Additionally, a greater number of chronic diseases was associated with higher odds of being in a higher vaccine-dose category (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.02-1.18).ConclusionDespite pandemic efforts, substantial ethnic disparities in COVID-19 vaccine uptake persisted, with lower coverage in racialized and Indigenous groups. Addressing structural inequities, comorbidities, and misinformation is critical to achieving more equitable, culturally responsive vaccination strategies.

articles.title: Impact and cost-effectiveness of national implementation of rotavirus vaccination in Vietnam: A modeling study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42837896. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129220. BackgroundIn Vietnam, rotavirus remains a leading cause of severe acute gastroenteritis resulting in hospitalization. Although rotavirus vaccines are available in the private sector-primarily accessible to urban children-the Expanded Programme on Immunization has only piloted the vaccine in select provinces. This study assessed the impact and cost-effectiveness of national rotavirus vaccination in Vietnam to inform policy decision on nationwide implementation.MethodsWe used a transparent static cohort model with a granular weekly age structure (< 5 years) to project rotavirus gastroenteritis (RVGE) cases, visits, hospitalizations, and deaths in children under five years, comparing no vaccination to nationwide vaccination with the domestic ROTAVIN vaccine over 10 years starting in 2026. Model inputs drew from global, regional, and local data including pre-vaccine incidence in Vietnam, local vaccine effectiveness and waning data, and treatment costs (governmental and societal perspectives) sourced from a local cost of illness study and hospital records (converted to 2025 USD). Deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses addressed parameter uncertainty.ResultsOver ten years, ROTAVIN vaccination was projected to reduce RVGE health burden by 42%, averting 97,776 (95% uncertainty interval 72,722-342,311) hospital admissions and 433 (330-1300) deaths. The program would cost US$39.5 million ($30.7-$117.7 million) for ten birth cohorts (2026-2036). From the governmental perspective, at least 62% of vaccination costs would be offset by healthcare savings. The cost per DALY averted was estimated at $982 (governmental perspective), while the program was cost-saving from the societal perspective in the base case. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness, with a 99% probability of cost-effectiveness from the governmental perspective at a willingness-to-pay threshold of 0.5 times Vietnam's GDP per capita (and 100% from the societal perspective).ConclusionsNationwide ROTAVIN vaccination could avert a substantial health and economic burden in Vietnam and would be highly cost-effective given recently published thresholds.

articles.title: Safety and immunogenicity of Thailand Government Pharmaceutical Organization (GPO) produced, COVID-19 vaccine, 10 μg HXP-GPOVac: A Phase III, double-blind, randomized trial in comparison with VAXZEVRIA.
articles.summary: PMID: 42869875. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129230. BackgroundHXP-GPOVac is a Thailand-produced, egg-based, inactivated recombinant Newcastle disease virus (NDV)-chimera vaccine expressing a membrane-anchored, prefusion-stabilized SARS-CoV-2 spike (NDV-HXP-S), developed to expand vaccine access. This phase III trial evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of a single HXP-GPOVac dose in healthy or clinically stable Thai adults who had completed a two-dose primary series of an authorized COVID-19 vaccine.MethodsIn this double-blind, randomized, active-controlled trial in Nakhon Phanom, Thailand, 4000 participants were randomized 3:1 to receive HXP-GPOVac or VAXZEVRIA (AstraZeneca, ChAdOx1 nCoV-19). Safety outcomes included incidence, severity, and vaccine-relatedness of adverse events (AEs). AE incidence was compared between vaccine groups using Chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Immunogenicity was assessed by pseudovirus neutralization assay for 50% neutralizing antibody titers (NT50) and ELISA for anti-Spike IgG. Non-inferiority was prespecified for NT50-based endpoints at day 14, defined by (i) a geometric mean concentration (GMC) ratio (HXP-GPOVac/VAXZEVRIA) with 95% CI lower bound >0.67 and (ii) a seroconversion rate (SCR) difference with 95% CI lower bound > -10%.ResultsSolicited AEs occurred in 43.7% of HXP-GPOVac recipients versus 53.5% of VAXZEVRIA recipients (p = 0.01). Most solicited AEs were mild. No vaccine-related serious AEs were reported. At day 14, the NT50 GMC ratio (HXP-GPOVac/VAXZEVRIA) was 0.83 (95% CI lower bound: 0.74), and the SCR difference was -2.35% (95% CI lower bound: -8.72%), both meeting non-inferiority criteria.ConclusionHXP-GPOVac was well-tolerated and demonstrated non-inferior immunogenicity compared with VAXZEVRIA at 14 days after vaccination. These findings provide rationale for larger studies to assess HXP-GPOVac clinical efficacy.

articles.title: Cost-effectiveness of universal infant hepatitis B vaccination programme in Finland.
articles.summary: PMID: 42887417. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129171. ObjectivesTo evaluate the cost-effectiveness of a universal infant hepatitis B vaccination programme in Finland.MethodsA static cohort model was employed to compare the health care costs and health effects of a universal infant hepatitis B vaccination programme with the present targeted vaccination programme. Estimates of hepatitis B incidence and hepatitis B-related costs were derived from national register data. The estimated hepatitis B incidence took into account acute asymptomatic infections. An annual discount rate of 3% was applied to costs and health effects and the main outcome measure was cost per quality adjusted life year (QALY) gained. We present the results with different price differences per dose of hexavalent and pentavalent vaccines. Sensitivity analyses identified influential inputs in the cost-effectiveness analysis.ResultsWe estimated 41 acute cases with every fifth being symptomatic, three chronic hepatitis B cases, and three hepatitis B-related deaths in a birth cohort of 58,000 children. The corresponding health care costs were ϵ46,400 and QALYs lost 14.4. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICER) were between ϵ24,500 and ϵ162,900 when the price difference per dose of pentavalent versus hexavalent vaccine was between two and 12 euros. The results were sensitive to hepatitis B incidence, vaccine cost, and discount rate.ConclusionsIn a very low hepatitis B prevalence country such as Finland, a universal infant hepatitis B vaccination programme appears justifiable use of public health care resources only with a very small price difference between pentavalent and hexavalent vaccines.

articles.title: rVSV-ΔG-EBOV-GP-Nipah-G (also designated PHV02) replication-competent, recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine for prevention of Nipah virus disease: Standardized template with key considerations for a risk/benefit assessment.
articles.summary: PMID: 42869683. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129113. A recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) expressing the glycoprotein (GP) of Ebola virus (rVSV-EBOV GP) has been approved for preventive immunization against Ebola (Ervebo®, Merck & Co.). The rVSV-EBOV vector was modified to express an additional glycoprotein (G) of Nipah virus (NiV), a bat-borne henipavirus endemic/epidemic in South and Southeast Asia that causes fatal encephalitis and pneumonia. The rVSV-EBOV-GP-NiV G vaccine candidate ("PHV02") is a unique chimeric virus with tropism and immunological properties derived from the wild-type (wt) vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) parent, the rVSV-EBOV-GP vector and the NiV G transgene donor. The EBOV GP enables fusion with the cell membrane and virus entry, whereas the NiV G protein mediates attachment to cells and serves as the antigen for stimulating NiV-specific immunity. This review focuses on the characteristics of the vector and vaccine candidate relevant to clinical and environmental safety, immunogenicity and efficacy. The Brighton Collaboration Benefit-Risk Assessment of VAccines by TechnolOgy (BRAVATO) standardized template is used to update the key characteristics and risks of the rVSV-EBOV vector (previously published [1]) and the novel PHV02 NiV vaccine candidate which is now in clinical trials. The template provides a rich source of information and guide to the supporting literature. While analogies of the PHV02 NiV vaccine to the backbone rVSV-EBOV vector are useful given the more extensive data available on the vector, the template emphasizes that PHV02 is a novel construct from a regulatory perspective and targets a different disease with unique characteristics and pathogenesis. Where similarities and parallels are drawn between nonclinical and clinical outcomes of rVSV-EBOV (vector) and PHV02 (vaccine), the reader should be cognizant of the limitations of these conclusions. The intended use of the standardized template is to provide a cohesive reference allowing vaccine developers and regulatory reviewers to understand characteristics, benefits and risks of a new vaccine candidate against NiV relevant to its future use in human populations, and to compare and contrast these characteristics to an approved vaccine constructed from the same (rVSV) vector system against a different indication (ebolavirus). The systematized template structure should facilitate utility of the paper.

articles.title: Waning immunity, an age shift, and rising adult burden of varicella after two decades of single-dose vaccination in South Korea.
articles.summary: PMID: 42879902. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129240. BackgroundMany countries have not adopted universal varicella vaccination (UVV), citing concerns that it could shift disease burden toward older, higher-risk age groups and be insufficiently cost-effective. Long-term data under sustained single-dose vaccination remain scarce. We assessed the immunological, epidemiological, and healthcare cost consequences of two decades of South Korea's single-dose National Immunization Program, which has maintained >95% coverage since 2005 without the anticipated decline in incidence.MethodsWe analyzed varicella-zoster virus immunoglobulin G titers in 3765 healthcare personnel (HCP) by birth group. We also examined national surveillance (Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency) and insurance claims (Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service) data from 2010 to 2024.ResultsSeronegativity was highest among HCP born during 1990-1994 (adjusted odds ratio, 3.83), and geometric mean titers declined across successive birth groups (geometric mean ratio, 0.70 [95% confidence interval, 0.63-0.77], 2000-2004 vs. pre-1980), indicating waning immunity. In 2024, adolescents surpassed children aged <10 years as the largest proportion of cases for the first time. Age-specific incidence rates increased approximately ninefold in adolescents and threefold in adults while remaining unchanged in children. Among adults, the proportion of varicella meningitis cases rose from 16.4% to 72.9%, and their share of varicella-related healthcare costs rose from 21.2% to 41.9%.ConclusionsAfter two decades of sustained high single-dose coverage, these findings provide evidence relevant to concerns about age shift and disease severity in settings yet to adopt UVV and support reassessment of the single-dose schedule.

articles.title: Circular RNA vaccines encoding Pvs25 induce antibodies that block Plasmodium vivax transmission.
articles.summary: PMID: 42849225. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129221. Plasmodium vivax is a major malaria parasite that causes acute illness in millions of people each year. Transmission-blocking vaccines (TBVs) could contribute substantially to malaria elimination, although none has yet been approved. We previously demonstrated that a nucleoside-modified mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccine targeting Pvs25, a leading P. vivax TBV antigen, elicited potent and durable transmission-blocking immunity in mice. Emerging evidence suggests that circular RNA (circRNA) may enhance RNA stability, prolong antigen expression, and potentially reduce manufacturing costs compared with conventional linear mRNA. We therefore developed and evaluated two circular Pvs25 RNA-LNP vaccines: one encoding wild-type Pvs25 and another encoding Pvs25 fused to the MHC class I trafficking domain (MITD). Their immunogenicity and functional activity were compared with those of a linear nucleoside-modified Pvs25 mRNA-LNP vaccine. In mice, a single immunization with either the circular RNA or linear mRNA Pvs25 vaccine induced detectable Pvs25-specific antibodies, while booster immunization substantially increased antibody titers and resulted in complete inhibition of P. vivax development in mosquitoes. Both vaccines also elicited robust Pvs25-specific antibody-secreting cell response and cytokine-producing cellular responses. Together, these findings demonstrate the potential of circRNA as a platform for malaria vaccine development and support further evaluation in non-human primates.

articles.title: Reconsidering vaccinate-to-live strategies in EU foot-and-mouth disease control.
articles.summary: PMID: 42837894. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129217. In January 2025, FMD was detected in water buffalos near Berlin. A few weeks later, a different FMDV-strain was confirmed on dairy farms in Slovakia and Hungary. Since February 2026, Cyprus and Lesvos are confronted with FMD-outbreaks. While Europe is rethinking its FMD-strategies, the two affected member states, Cyprus and Greece, take opposite approaches to control the disease. FMD-vaccination was pivotal for its eradication in many parts of the world. Such regions fought new outbreaks by traditional animal-disease-control. In 2001, a devastating FMD-epizootic swept across the UK and continental Europe. Several million sheep, cattle, and pigs were culled. In the aftermath, OIE (now: WOAH) and EU revised their FMD-strategies. Now, WOAH's Terrestrial Animal Health Code puts strong emphasis on reactive vaccination. An FMD-free status can be regained without slaughtering all vaccinated animals. By contrast, the European FMD Directive of 2003, which contained similar provisions, was repealed. Under the new Delegated Regulation, all restrictions on a vaccination zone are upheld until the last vaccinated animal is removed. Cyprus implemented country-wide FMD-vaccination despite these restrictions. Fearing trade barriers, Greece decided not to vaccinate. Were the consequences not so dramatic, a better head-to-head comparison would hardly be conceivable. Modern FMD-vaccines induce robust immunity after just seven days, minimize virus transmission and allow for DIVA strategies. In addition to the risks posed by global trade and travel, Europe faces major social, economic, and geopolitical challenges. The risk of FMDV incursions is imminent. Cyprus can afford to live with trade restrictions, because export of live animals, raw dairy products and fresh meat only play a minor role in its economy. This would be entirely different if livestock-dense regions in the heart of the continent were affected. The EU must not forgo highly effective and ethically superior control measures that could mitigate socio-economic consequences of future FMD-outbreaks.

articles.title: Mobile-app-based cohort event monitoring study (CEM) of COVID-19 vaccines.
articles.summary: PMID: 42843285. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129219. Vaccine pharmacovigilance is critically important to ensure transparent information related to vaccine safety. We conducted a prospective, non-interventional, population-based cohort study, SafeVac2.0, in order to supplement passive surveillance of COVID-19 vaccines by collecting self-reported adverse events (AEs). Participation via smartphone app was allowed within 48 h after the administration of the first or second dose of a COVID-19 vaccine. Adverse events were collected up to 3 weeks after the first vaccination, 8 weeks after the second vaccination, and 7 days after the booster dose. Participants were also asked about their health condition 6 and 12 months after the first dose registered. The study was conducted from December 26, 2020 to September 30, 2022. A total of 739,216 persons met the primary inclusion criteria, of which 732,864 documented at least one vaccination. Data on 1,436,039 vaccinations were collected. At least one AE was reported for 68% of the vaccinations and in total 4,007,149 AEs were reported. 88% of AEs consisted of solicited local and systemic reactogenicity. Age, sex, vaccine product and dose were potential predictors for solicited adverse events. The need for medical care was reported in 0.36% of vaccinations. Overall, the study results provide reassurance of the safety profile of COVID-19 vaccines. The use of a native app to monitor self-reported adverse events represents an innovative pharmacovigilance approach.

articles.title: Understanding rotavirus vaccine acceptance in Indonesia: a WHO BeSD-based exploration of parents' and religious leaders' perspectives in three provinces.
articles.summary: PMID: 42879900. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129211. BackgroundDisparities in rotavirus vaccine uptake in Indonesia persist despite its national implementation, yet, the community-level determinants of vaccination remain underexplored. Understanding the behavioural and social factors influencing vaccination decisions is essential for developing interventions that improve vaccine uptake in the community.MethodsA qualitative study was conducted using the World Health Organization Behavioural and Social Drivers (WHO BeSD) framework. Data were collected between May and December 2025 through five focus group discussions and 24 in-depth interviews with parents and religious leaders in Yogyakarta, Bali, and the Moluccas. Participants were purposively sampled to capture diverse experiences and perspectives. Data were analysed using a deductive thematic approach guided by the four BeSD domains: Thinking and Feeling, Social Processes, Motivation, and Practical Issues.ResultsSeventy-one participants (61 parents and 10 religious leaders) took part in the study. Overall acceptance of rotavirus vaccination was high and driven by trust in vaccine benefits and confidence in health services. Within the Thinking and Feeling domain, participants recognised the severity of diarrhoeal disease and the protective value of vaccination, although concerns about adverse effects and limited access to information remained, particularly in rural areas. Social Processes generally supported vaccine uptake through health workers' recommendations, community endorsement, and support from religious leaders. Most mothers reported autonomy in vaccination decision-making, although gender-related influences persisted in some households. Motivation to vaccinate was strengthened by the desire to protect children from severe illness. Under Practical Issues, participants described vaccination services as accessible through primary healthcare facilities but highlighted the need for improved information dissemination and more reliable vaccine availability in remote areas.ConclusionsImproving vaccine literacy, strengthening service delivery, and addressing practical barriers are critical to increasing complete rotavirus vaccination uptake. Tailored communication and engagement of parents, religious leaders, and community stakeholders may further enhance vaccine acceptance and uptake across diverse Indonesian settings.

articles.title: Protection of Omicron XBB.1.5 vaccine, previous infection, and their induced neutralizing antibodies against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection during Omicron KP.3 wave.
articles.summary: PMID: 42879903. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129242. BackgroundData are limited on the protection of Omicron XBB.1.5 vaccine, previous infection, and their induced neutralizing antibodies against Omicron KP.3 infection.MethodsAmong 1826 tertiary hospital staff in Tokyo who had received three or more doses of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines and provided blood samples in June 2024, we prospectively examined the associations of XBB.1.5 vaccination and previous infection (classified by the timing of the last infection as pre-Omicron XBB, Omicron XBB, or Omicron JN.1 waves) with the risk of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection during the Omicron KP.3 wave (June to September 2024). In a nested case-control analysis, we compared pre-infection live-virus KP.3.3-neutralizing antibody titers between cases and 1: 1 propensity-score matched controls.ResultsXBB.1.5 vaccination was not associated with measurable protection against symptomatic infection (4%, 95% CI, -88 to 51). Previous infection conferred protection that increased with its recency: 26% (95% CI, -26 to 56) for pre-Omicron XBB, 44% (95% CI, 2 to 68) for Omicron XBB, and 89% (95% CI, 52 to 97) for Omicron JN.1 waves. articles.summary: PMID: 42858679. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129239. articles.title: Longitudinal SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine immunogenicity in inflammatory bowel disease in relation to anti-TNF therapy and age: a prospective cohort study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42849224. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129224. BackgroundPatients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) on immunomodulatory therapy may respond less well to vaccination. We followed humoral and cellular responses to SARS-CoV-2 vaccination over 12 months.MethodsIn this single-centre, prospective cohort study, adults with IBD received mRNA vaccine under the Austrian national programme. articles.title: Assessment of the Fasciola hepatica saposin-like protein 2 (rFhSAP2) vaccine candidate in sheep: Immunogenicity without protective efficacy.
articles.summary: PMID: 42837893. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129223. Gallbladder-derived egg viability was lower in vaccinated sheep (56.9%) than in the infection control (75.9%) and adjuvant control (73.6%) groups (p > 0.05). Vaccination induced a strong and sustained humoral response. IgG and IgG1 levels were significantly higher in vaccinated sheep than in both control groups from weeks 4-24 and 4-32, respectively. IgG2 levels were also significantly higher from weeks 4-24, although the response was lower than that of IgG1. Overall, rtFhSAP2 formulated with Montanide ISA 201 VG was highly immunogenic in sheep, but the humoral response did not translate into significant protection against F. hepatica.
